Learning Objectives
Identify indications for surgical management using local anesthesia with epinephrine
(occasionally referred to as wide awake local anesthesia with no tourniquet or WALANT).
Evaluate the potential advantages and disadvantages of various mixtures of lidocaine,
bupivacaine, epinephrine, and bicarbonate and different needle sizes.
Apply techniques for the administration of local anesthesia, for a digital block, and to limit
bleeding without a tourniquet.
Recognize the potential advantages and disadvantages of wide awake local anesthesia with no
tourniquet during various types of upper extremity surgery.

Local anesthesia has been in use for more than 100 years.
Traditional teaching was that epinephrine should not be used in combination with lidocaine or
other local anesthetic agents because of the associated risk of ischemia to the soft tissues,
particularly in the fingers and toes, penis and nose.
The first local anesthetic to be used in the finger was procaine.
It was developed in 1903 to replace cocaine and remained the most widely used injectable
local anesthetic agent until lidocaine was introduced in 1948.
Finger ischemia associated with the use of procaine was falsely attributed to its combination
with epinephrine; the problem more likely was related to the relatively low pH of procaine
(3.6), which is even lower if stored on a shelf for a prolonged period.1,2
In 1948, the FDA published a warning in the Journal of the American Medical Association that
batches of Novocain with a pH of 1 had been identified. This would amount to injecting a
strong acid into human tissues.
In 1959, the FDA instituted mandatory expiration dates for injectable medicines.
Dr. Donald Lalonde—credited with the recent popularization of surgical management with the
use of local anesthetic alone—learned the technique as a resident from notable Canadian
hand surgeons, including Pat Shoemaker, Bob MacFarlane, and John Fielding.
A review of evidence from 1880 to 2000 did not find a single report of a complication from the
use of epinephrine as an adjunct to lidocaine for local anesthesia in the finger.3
Practical Use
Most residents and fellows first use local anesthetic agents in the emergency room to manage
fingertip injuries or injuries on the dorsum of the hand and forearm in which hemostasis is
easier to maintain with pressure.
Traditional use involves injecting margins of the cut in the hand or forearm with 1% or 2%
lidocaine 1:100,000 or 1:200,000 with epinephrine.
Because the maximum dose of lidocaine is 7 mg/kg, a surgeon rarely would approach toxic
levels of lidocaine in adults.
For example, using 1% lidocaine 1:100,000 with epinephrine in a 70-kg patient, surgeons could
safely inject 49 mL or 490 mg before approaching a toxic serum level of lidocaine.
In most patients, a 10 mL syringe and a 25-gauge needle are used.
Buffering with 8.4% sodium bicarbonate also may reduce the pain of injection, achieved by
adding approximately 1 mL of bicarbonate solution to the 10 mL of 1% lidocaine with
epinephrine already contained within a syringe.

The use of a smaller needle in combination with bicarbonate results in substantially less pain.4
In the finger, a single injection just proximal to the flexion crease at the base of the finger will
anesthetize both digital nerves and the dorsal cutaneous branches of the digital nerve,
producing adequate anesthesia to the palmar surface of the finger and the dorsal surface at
the distal interphalangeal joint, including the fingertip.
For a wound on the forearm, a recommended technique is to use a large enough volume of
local anesthetic so that soft-tissue swelling occurs and the effect on the skin can be visualized
and felt (so-called tumescent anesthesia).
If concern for digital pallor exists, the epinephrine can be reversed via phentolamine injection.
In general, phentolamine (2 to 5 mg) is reconstituted in saline and injected in the same region
that the epinephrine was injected.5
Alternatively, phenoxybenzamine may be used. If available, phenoxybenzamine is as effective
as phentolamine and can be administered by mouth.
Outpatient Surgical Setting
Potential advantages of surgical management with local anesthesia include:
Avoids the potential harms and adverse effects of general or regional anesthesia
Ability to counsel the patient on recovery during the procedure
During tendon repair, patients can observe the repair and visualize their finger moving again.
Similarly, the surgeon can determine if the repair impinges on a pulley to determine the need
for release of A2 or A4. If a gap is noted at the repair site with active motion, additional
sutures may be added.
Patients who are not good candidates for wide awake surgery, such as those who may not
cooperate during anesthesia, may be allowed to wake up enough during the procedure to
move the finger and allow for the same decision-making regarding tendon gap and excursion
after repair.
Because epinephrine affords a relatively blood-free field, a tourniquet or sedation to
eliminate tourniquet pain are not necessary. In combination with site marking and a pre-
procedure timeout, wrong site surgery may be less likely because the patient is awake and a
part of the ongoing dialogue with the surgeon and team during the procedure.
Patients spend less time in the recovery area and often can drive themselves home after
certain minor procedures in which the hand remains functional.
Lower cost and resource use. Surgical management can be performed in the office with the
use of local field drapes and a set of sterile instruments.

Much less solid waste disposal
Medical optimization, laboratory tests, and electrocardiography are uncommonly necessary.
Patients with high co-pays and deductibles have much less out-of-pocket expenses.
The patient does not need to change into a gown. Exposure of the surgical site is sufficient,
and many surgeons use field sterility, in which draping material is minimized.
Discontinuation of anticoagulation for hand surgical procedures usually is not necessary, and
the use of epinephrine helps minimize bleeding, resulting in a manageable surgical field
without the need for a tourniquet.
Potential disadvantages of surgical management under local anesthesia include:
Uncomfortable patient positioning for a lengthy procedure without sedation.
Risk of notable bleeding and difficulty attaining control (eg, damage to the radial artery in
removing a volar wrist ganglion).
Applications
Flexor Tendon Repair
General anesthesia or sedation and regional were typically blocks used for flexor tendon
repair to keep the patient still as the tendon is sutured. Prolonged tourniquet use and supine
positioning are difficult.
A cooperative, non-sedated patient will hold still as the tendon is sutured. After repair, the
patient can actively flex and extend the finger so the surgeon can verify satisfactory active
finger motion without restriction of the repair site as it passes through the annular pulleys.
A serendipitous finding of the surgeon observing the patient actively flexing and extending the
finger after tendon repair is that the entire A4 pulley one-half to two-thirds of the distal A2
pulley can be released without bowstring.
If a gap is present at the repair site, the surgeon can reinforce the repair with the use of
additional sutures to avoid additional gapping or complete rupture of the repair.
Local anesthetic agent is applied first as a digital block and then as a field block to limit
bleeding throughout the surgical dissection.
Ideally, the surgeon should wait 30 minutes for the epinephrine to take effect before beginning
the procedure; otherwise visualization can be counterintuitively decreased from anesthetic
infiltration.
The palm should be injected at the most likely site for retrieval of the retracted tendon.

Anesthetic should be administered with the patient in the supine position for maximal
relaxation and to prevent a vasovagal reaction.
If the patient becomes lightheaded despite supine positioning, elevate the lower extremities,
and monitor the patient closely.
In the patients with a flexor tendon laceration in the palm of the hand, begin with a median
nerve block at the wrist, wait at least 10 minutes for the block to become effective, then inject
the palm of the hand via the tumescent technique for the proposed site of the surgical
incision.
Tendon Transfer
Theoretically, all transfers can be performed with the use of the local anesthetic techniques
already described.
An ideal transfer under local anesthetic is the extensor indicis proprius to extensor pollicis
longus. Video 1 shows physical examination of bilateral hands of a 45-year-old guitarist who
suffered a spontaneous rupture of the left extensor pollicis longus, which is observed as lack
of interphalangeal joint extension in the left hand.
Proposed incisions over the dorsum of the wrist, thumb, and index finger
metacarpophalangeal joint are injected via tumescent technique 30 minutes preoperatively.
The initial incision is made at the base of the thumb to identify the distal stump of the
extensor pollicis longus.
The extensor indicis proprius is identified and usually is the ulnar of the two tendons at the
metacarpophalangeal joint. To confirm this tendon is the extensor indicis proprius , it is
exposed at the level of the extensor retinaculum, the location at which it is always the ulnar of
the two extrinsic extensors to the index finger. The distal tendon is divided, with care taken to
preserve the sagittal band, and then transferred subcutaneously over the extensor
retinaculum and secured to the distal tendon via a Pulvertaft weave. Tension is set under
normal physiologic muscle tone; this differs from procedures performed under general
anesthesia or regional anesthesia, in which the muscle being transferred is under lower
tone. Video 2 shows intraoperative physiologic tensioning of the transfer. Excess tension can
be débrided.
(Video 3) shows active thumb extension at 3 months postoperatively, which is comparable
with that of the contralateral side. The patient resumed playing the guitar 6 weeks
postoperatively.

Tenolysis
If healing flexor or extensor tendons adhere to surrounding structures, such as other tendons,
skin, or bone, release of these adhesions may help regain motion.
Wide awake local anesthesia with no tourniquet is ideal for tenolysis because the patient
remains awake and cooperative throughout the procedure, allowing the surgeon to evaluate
the results of the procedure in real time and allowing the patient to experience and visualize
return of active range of motion immediately in the operating room.
Infiltration of local anesthetic through revision incisions and scar tissue may be more
challenging and requires additional patience and time.
Potential Obstacles
Shifting to local anesthesia is a considerable cultural change in most outpatient settings.
Injection of the local anesthetic in the preoperative holding area is a procedure that merits its
own time-out.
Anesthesiology personnel may be concerned about lost revenue if an increasing percentage of
procedures are performed under local anesthesia.

Contraindications
Allergic reaction to lidocaine is rare. Options include preoperative allergy consultation or use
of an alternative local anesthetic. Toxicity is more common but still rare, and surgeons should
be familiar with its management.
Patients with preexisting vascular disease in the finger, such as Burger disease, are not good
candidates for wide awake local anesthesia with no tourniquet technique. Circulation is poor in
these patients, and vasoconstriction may result in irreversible thrombosis of the
microcirculation. Such patients likely are better candidates for regional blocks, such as axillary
block or general anesthesia.
In rare patients in whom marked pallor is present, patients in whom puncture of the tip of the
digit does not elicit bleeding, and patients in whom a previously underappreciated vascular
pathology is identified, phentolamine may be used to reverse the effect of epinephrine.
1 to 2 mg of phentolamine mixed into 2 to 5 mL of saline is injected into the area of skin pallor
to reverse the effect of epinephrine on circulation.
Occasionally, phenoxybenzamine administered can be administered orally with success,
particularly in the management of accidental self-administered injection with the use of an
epinephrine autoinjector.
Technical factors are important to consider to avoid potential complications. Surgeons should
avoid injection of excessive volumes into enclosed areas, which may essentially create a
compartment syndrome problem. For example, injection into the flexor sheath should be
avoided, and injection of local anesthesia with epinephrine should be performed cautiously
distal to the palmodigital crease. Similarly, lidocaine with epinephrine should be avoided or
used with caution in patients with fixed or dynamic vascular compromise, such as those with
peripheral vascular disease or Raynaud disease or phenomenon; surgeons should be
prepared to reverse the epinephrine via phentolamine injection.
Patients must be educated on the care of anesthetized body parts postoperatively. Because
the digit or part is numb, patients may inadvertently expose the digit or part to excessive heat
or cold and cause thermal injury. Similarly, because of the numbness, trauma may go
undetected. Patients should be advised that the numbness will resolve with time alone and
attempts to wake the part up by soaking it in hot water may result in devastating injury
because of thermal injury. These types of injuries may manifest as digital necrosis in adjacent
digits at the same watermark level, which is different than that observed with true vascular
insufficiency, in which necrosis would be observed at various levels.

Complications
Although rare, complications can occur. The most common complication is pain at the
injection site, which usually resolves in 2 or 3 days. Rarely, blistering and changes
consistent with ischemia may be observed.6 Such changes and similar complications
may result from the patient coming in contact with a hot object, such as very hot water,
while the finger is still numb; an overly tight dressing; the lidocaine; some toxin in the
solution; or an infectious agent, such as group B streptococcus. No procedure is risk
free.
